reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: The most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract, thought to arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, most often in the stomach and next most often in the small intestine
Most are driven by activating mutations in the KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinases, and KIT immunostaining is the diagnostic hallmark
Presentation ranges from an incidental finding to vague abdominal discomfort, a palpable mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration
On endoscopy they typically appear as a smooth submucosal bulge with normal overlying mucosa, sometimes with central umbilication
Malignant potential is estimated mainly from tumour size and mitotic rate together with anatomical site, rather than being simply benign or malignant
Surgical resection with negative margins is the mainstay of treatment for localised disease, and routine lymph node dissection is generally unnecessary because nodal spread is rare
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting KIT/PDGFRA have transformed management of advanced, metastatic, or high-risk disease and are used in adjuvant and neoadjuvant settings
Biopsy should be approached cautiously because of bleeding and rupture risk; endoscopic ultrasound-guided sampling is often preferred when tissue is needed
The liver and peritoneum are the usual sites of metastatic spread
reference.pathophysiology: GISTs originate from or resemble the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the gut. Gain-of-function mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene, or less commonly in PDGFRA, produce constitutive receptor tyrosine kinase signalling that drives uncontrolled proliferation. A minority are wild-type for these genes and involve alternative pathways such as succinate dehydrogenase deficiency, which is more common in younger patients and in syndromic disease. Tumours grow as submucosal or intramural masses; larger and more mitotically active lesions have greater potential for haematogenous spread, particularly to the liver and peritoneal surfaces.
additionalDifferentials: Leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma of the gut
Gastric or small-bowel adenocarcinoma or lymphoma
Extrinsic compression from an adjacent mass
Pancreatic or splenic lesion mimicking a gastric submucosal mass
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound to characterise the submucosal lesion and guide sampling
Contrast-enhanced CT for staging, size assessment, and detection of liver or peritoneal metastases
Immunohistochemistry for KIT (CD117) and DOG1 to confirm the diagnosis
Mutational analysis of KIT and PDGFRA to guide targeted therapy and predict response
Mitotic count and tumour size assessment for risk stratification
redFlags: Large tumour with high mitotic rate indicating high malignant potential and need for oncological management
Significant or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from an ulcerated tumour
Tumour rupture (spontaneous or during biopsy) causing peritoneal dissemination and haemoperitoneum
New liver or peritoneal lesions signalling metastatic progression
reference.prognosis: Small, low-mitotic-rate, completely resected tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas large or mitotically active lesions carry a substantial risk of recurrence and metastasis. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival in advanced disease, though resistance can develop over time.
pitfalls: Assuming a submucosal lesion is benign without adequate risk stratification by size and mitotic rate
Performing incautious biopsy of a friable tumour and precipitating bleeding or rupture
Omitting mutational testing, which can predict poor response to standard targeted therapy
Confusing a GIST with other spindle-cell tumours when immunohistochemistry is not performed
management: Resect localised tumours completely with negative margins, avoiding routine lymph node dissection as nodal spread is rare
Use the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib as adjuvant therapy for higher-risk tumours and as first-line treatment for advanced or metastatic disease
Guide targeted therapy by KIT and PDGFRA mutational analysis, selecting avapritinib for the imatinib-resistant PDGFRA D842V genotype
Switch to later-line tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib and regorafenib on resistance or progression
Stratify recurrence risk by tumour size, mitotic rate, and anatomical site to guide adjuvant therapy
Survey with contrast-enhanced CT for local recurrence and hepatic or peritoneal metastases
Manage within a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team
